memory_block.body: Referral incentives performed well in established customers, adding qualified revenue without measurable harm to retention.
Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.
Shortening onboarding improved completion rates and time-to-value, lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts.

Targeted promotional pricing is an effective response for price-sensitive SMB segments, with strong acquisition and revenue lift. However, it materially reduced 30-day retention; do not generalize it as a growth strategy.
Enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows; the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality.
Activation messaging inside the product improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action.

answer.rationale: The two observed declines are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), which points at the funnel itself rather than at price. memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer signup fields lifted first-week activation) both target exactly the metrics that regressed, and memory_91 is the close alternative. I want the archived records for memory_86 and memory_91 because both were measured on early-funnel outcomes only; I need to know whether either was ever tracked out to retention or qualified revenue, and whether memory_86's lift was on a self-serve population comparable to today's. The competitor's entry pricing makes promotional_pricing the tempting response, but memory_73 explicitly records that it bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and warns against generalizing it, which is disqualifying against a sustainable-long-term-revenue objective; I do not need to spend budget re-verifying a memory whose caveat already rules it out. referral_incentive (memory_57) is sound but addresses established customers, not the activation gap. enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment entirely and would not move these numbers this week. Downstream risk to flag: removing signup fields or onboarding steps can shift the harm downstream the same way discounting did — you can raise completion while admitting less-qualified accounts or skipping the steps that create real time-to-value, so completion improves and 30-day retention and revenue quality quietly degrade. I therefore treat memory_86's lift as established only for completion and early adoption, not for sustainable qualified revenue, and will run this with retention and qualified-revenue guardrails and a holdout rather than shipping it broadly on inherited confidence.
